description:
Stand up a multi-node cluster, run a workload against it, and randomly kill things -- processes frequently, whole nodes less often -- to find out what breaks. Then diagnose it and file it.

## Why this is worth building

Bedrock is designed to survive component failure: the Director monitors every data-plane singleton it spawns, and a :DOWN on any of them (except the distributor) is epoch-fatal, forcing a fresh recovery. That machinery is exercised today only by single-BEAM unit tests against mock clusters. bedrock-q67.49 already records the lesson -- 'every blocking defect was a composition failure invisible to the unit suite'. ../bedrock_ex's ISSUES.md is a list of real multi-node failures found by a human sending SIGTERM and reading logs: cross-node worker init failures, orphaned workers, silent commit failures.

## The hard part is the oracle, not the killing

Randomly killing processes in a system built to recover mostly produces noise. The harness is only worth having if it can tell a survivable fault from a real defect. Four falsifiable invariants:

1. Acked-commit durability -- every commit the client acked is journaled externally and must be readable afterward. Catches the silent commit failures bedrock_ex observed.
2. Conservation -- a transfer workload whose total is invariant at every snapshot version. Catches lost writes, torn transactions, MVCC violations.
3. Liveness -- after faults stop, the cluster serves again within a bound. Catches wedged recovery and epoch thrash.
4. Independent data consistency -- offline tooling reads object storage and verifies it without asking the cluster anything. Self-reported health is precisely the signal a chaos harness cannot trust.

## Diagnosis is what makes it useful

A failure must reduce to something a person can act on: a seed (the whole fault schedule is a pure function of seed + config), an on-disk journal of faults and ops written as they happen so a wedged cluster still leaves evidence, captured telemetry and per-node traces, and eventually shrinking -- replay the seed with faults progressively removed to find the minimal schedule that reproduces.

## Scope

Object storage is NOT a fault target -- assumed stable, MinIO in the harness proper. It IS a verification target; see the fsck children. v1 faults are process kills plus whole-node halt and restart-from-disk. Network partitions are deferred: partition semantics may be underspecified.

## Status

Phase 0 (bedrock-80f, PR #322) is done and green: three :peer nodes form a real cluster and serve a transaction from ExUnit. Successive PRs stack on that branch.

fsck is sequenced first: it is independent of the peer work, testable against a single node's output, and useful on its own as an operator tool even if the rest never ships.
title: [EPIC] Chaos-testing harness: find what breaks when processes and nodes die
